definition: Cupidity means an overpowering greed for wealth.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word cupidity. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know cupidity should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The board meeting turned tense when the founder proposed cutting safety inspections to widen profits - cupidity dressed up as efficiency, one engineer muttered.
Longing is any strong wish and can be perfectly innocent; there is nothing innocent about cupidity.
Greed is the broad vice of wanting too much of anything; cupidity sharpens it into an overpowering hunger for wealth in particular.

Covetousness is fixated wanting aimed at what already belongs to someone else - the neighbor's car, a rival's title. Cupidity needs no owner to rob: it is an overpowering hunger for wealth itself, whoever holds it, and it would be just as ravenous over unclaimed treasure.

Acquisitiveness is the collector's steady itch to obtain and add - more stamps, more sneakers, more of anything - and it can be harmless, even cheerful. Cupidity is neither mild nor neutral: a hunger for money so overpowering it has taken the person over, and the word itself accuses.

Avarice is miserly greed that clutches wealth and cannot let it go - the hoard counted nightly, the purse never opened. Cupidity points at the craving side: the overpowering hunger to seize wealth in the first place. Avarice grips what it has; cupidity reaches for more.

satisfaction with what one already has

Latin cupere, 'to desire,' lives on in English only inside this word - and in a name you already know: Cupid, the winged Roman god of desire who still shows up every February. Cupidity is that desire gone hard and hungry for gold.
Cupidity means an overpowering greed for wealth.
The lottery winner's cousin appeared within a week, full of investment ideas that all happened to route the money through his own accounts.
When the winner hesitated, the cousin dropped the pretense and simply demanded a share.
It was cupidity in its plainest form: not need, not a plan to build anything, just hunger for someone else's money.
Cupidity is narrower and harsher than greed: it is greed aimed specifically at wealth, and it carries the writer's judgment that the craving has taken the person over.
A dragon coiled on a pile of gold is the picture cupidity paints.
Cupidity is a courtroom-and-editorial word: it accuses.
Everyday speech says greed.
Reach for cupidity when the greed is specifically for money and you want the sentence to pass judgment - and note that despite the shared god, it has nothing to do with modern valentine romance.

The legend of El Dorado began modestly: a Colombian chief said to dust himself with gold for a lake ceremony.
In European retelling the gilded man swelled into a gilded city, and the city into an empire of gold waiting to be seized.
Expedition after expedition marched into the interior.
Chroniclers describe men abandoning farms, selling inheritances, and mortgaging their futures for a rumor.
One friar wrote that cupidity had hollowed the colonists out: the hunger for treasure was no longer a wish but a master, and it fed on wealth no one had ever seen.
There was, of course, no city.
The fortunes spent hunting it were real; so were the men the hunger used up.
